transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-20
Start time (UTC): 15:30
Duration: ~58m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), Greg Halvorsen (CTO - StormGate), Linda Park (Head of InfoSec), Tom Wu (Platform Eng)

--- Summary / Topics (auto) ---
High level: private (VPC) deployment review focused on airlock/egress, SOC 2 gap analysis, KMS handoff, RBAC/SSO mapping and audit log retention windows.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. With me is Ethan, our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Greg Halvorsen: Good, thanks. Ready to dive in, got Linda and Tom on my side.
[00:10] Linda Park: Hi, thanks. We've been looking at the private deployment notes, want to make sure the airlock approach fits our SOC 2 controls.
[00:16] Ethan Ross: Great — that's exactly what we planned to focus on today. We'll walk through a proposed VPC airlock pattern, ingress and egress proxies, KMS integration, and then map the bits to SOC 2/ISO controls at a high level.
[00:28] Tom Wu: Quick ask: we run in two regions and we need to keep everything within EU + US east for residency. Also our current KMS is CloudVault HSM — we will need to know how to handover keys for the private runtime.
[00:40] Maya Patel: Noted — thanks Tom. We'll cover KMS options and key management handoff.
[00:44] Linda Park: Also, retention for audit logs. Our SIEM requires 365 days with immutability for certain logs.
[00:51] Ethan Ross: We can stream audit events to your SIEM, and we have support for append-only logs via S3 object lock or external log collector, we'll show the integration.

[01:05] Ethan Ross: OK, starting with the airlock. Slide deck link: (shared) — the pattern we propose is a dedicated VPC with an isolated control plane in a private subnet, workers in dedicated subnets and an egress proxy in a hardened subnet that limits outbound flows to a small allowlist. The idea is that no worker can reach the public internet directly.
[01:26] Greg Halvorsen: So everything leaves through the proxy? We want to avoid any accidental outbound chatty calls. That aligns with our perimeter requirements.
[01:33] Ethan Ross: Exactly. We recommend a two-tiered egress: first go through the egress proxy (TLS inspected or mTLS), then if needed a NAT gateway owned by StormGate for allowed updates. There's also a fallback flow to a regional mirror inside Redwood's private peering if the NAT is unavailable.
[01:48] Linda Park: Fallback to Redwood peering — is that acceptable from a policy perspective? We have strict data-flow rules for PCI-adjacent workloads.
[01:56] Maya Patel: We discussed this during contracting — fallback is only to a customer-designated region and requires explicit enablement. If you need zero fallback, we can disable the public fallback and keep everything on-premises-only.
[02:10] Tom Wu: That may be required for the PCI-adjacent lanes. Can you show the routing tables?
[02:13] Ethan Ross: Yep — I'll pull up the network diagram. (pause) Alright, diagram: workers in private subnets, route 10.2.0.0/16 to the egress proxy, egress proxy ACLs restrict destination ports to our allowlist (TLS 443, KMS ports). Audit logs are shipped over an outbound TLS connection to your SIEM collector IPs on port 6514.
[02:33] Greg Halvorsen: How is TLS validated? Do you support mTLS with client certs from our CA?
[02:39] Ethan Ross: Yes, we support mTLS for mutual auth. We also integrate with customer-provided CA via the control plane secret store. For extra assurance we can add a hardware-backed client cert (HSM-generated) for the egress proxy.

[03:00] Linda Park: Let's talk about keys — CloudVault HSM is our KMS. What's the process for key derivation and rotation? We want to control key ops.
[03:08] Ethan Ross: Two models: 1) Envelope encryption with customer-managed master keys (CMK) — your KMS holds the root key, Redwood receives only wrapped keys; 2) HSM bring-your-own-key where private key materials never leave your HSM and Redwood acts as an operator that requests decryption via an API to your KMS over a private peering link. For SOC 2, option 2 is stronger since key material never moves.
[03:31] Tom Wu: The API approach is doable, we have an internal KMS endpoint reachable over peering. Latency on decryption call is something to watch for — will that impact inference latency?
[03:40] Ethan Ross: For per-request decryption that's expensive. We recommend caching decrypted key material in the runtime's local secure enclave (short lived) and using an HMAC-style sealing so we avoid roundtrips on every token. We also include a KV-cache layer for model KV cache that doesn't need encryption at the same granularity. But yes, design must balance latency and key exposure.
[03:58] Linda Park: So we still maintain key control, but runtime holds ephemeral keys in memory — we need proof that memory is wiped on process exit and that it cannot be paged to disk.
[04:08] Ethan Ross: Absolutely — the runtime uses mlock and enclave protections where available, and disk paging is disabled for those processes. We can provide the technical notes and memory-scrub proofs from our engineering team.

[04:28] Greg Halvorsen: On RBAC and SSO — we use SAML SSO (Okta) and expect role mapping to internal IAM groups. How granular can Redwood's console RBAC be when we run Private?
[04:38] Maya Patel: For Private deployments we offer the same RBAC surface as Hosted: role templates (admin, operator, auditor) and attribute-based mapping from SAML assertions. You can map Okta groups to roles and also lock down token issuance to certain IPs.
[04:51] Tom Wu: And audit logs for who requested model-run? We need end-to-end traces: user->job->model-version->response hash.
[04:59] Ethan Ross: That's in the plan. We emit per-request metadata: requestor identity (SAML subject), model id, model version, timestamp, pod id, and an event hash. Those events are forwarded to your SIEM and can be signed to prevent tampering.
[05:14] Linda Park: Signing sounds good — can we integrate with our log provenance ingestion?
[05:18] Ethan Ross: Yes — we can attach a detached signature per batch and you can verify in SIEM. We'll include sample implementation.

[05:40] Greg Halvorsen: On SOC 2 mapping specifically — where are the biggest gaps you've seen from similar customers?
[05:46] Maya Patel: Typically it's three areas: 1) key management and HSM integration — customers want stronger guarantees; 2) full audit trail mapping for model prompts/outputs to meet retention and immutability; 3) network egress and fallback policies — making sure there's no accidental outbound paths. We can show a control-matrix mapping.
[06:05] Linda Park: For immutability we want WORM storage for logs tied to a retention policy. Is Redwood supporting object-lock S3 or a write-once store?
[06:14] Ethan Ross: We support S3 object lock on the private deployment, or alternatively we can stream logs to your write-once archival location; both patterns are used.
[06:22] Tom Wu: How about data residency segregation at tenant level? We have multiple subsidiaries and can't co-mingle data across EU/US.
[06:29] Maya Patel: You can deploy separate private clusters per region or per tenant, pin them to specific AZs, and enforce routing to ensure data never crosses the boundary. There is a small operational cost to managing multiple clusters but it's the safest approach.

[06:50] Greg Halvorsen: Let's talk about performance. If we use HSM-wrapped keys and the egress proxy, what's the impact on token latency? Our SLO for the inference path is p95 < 120ms.
[06:59] Ethan Ross: We expect the network airlock to add minimal additional network hops. The HSM on-per-request decryption would be too slow — that's why we suggest envelope encryption with ephemeral local keys. With ephemeral caching and aggressive batching you can still meet p95 120ms for short prompts; very long context or heavy quantization changes behavior. We'll want to run a pilot with representative traffic to validate.
[07:24] Tom Wu: Pilot sounds good — we'd also like to test canary fallbacks. What happens if the egress proxy is misconfigured and blocks essential model downloads?
[07:33] Ethan Ross: There are layered controls: first is a pre-flight check during deployments that verifies allowlist egress rules; second is a canary deployment that attempts model pull and fails safely; third is an automated rollback if the runtime can't reach the model store. We'll show the runbook.
[07:49] Linda Park: Do you provide playbooks for incident response and audit evidence for SOC 2 audits?
[07:54] Maya Patel: Yes — we have incident response templates, evidence artifacts, and a SOC 2 package that includes control tests, logs, and change history. We'll attach the package in the follow-up.

[08:10] Greg Halvorsen: A few quick clarifications: 1) Is there an option for on-prem connector rather than full private cloud? 2) How does Redwood handle OS-level patches for the worker nodes?
[08:20] Ethan Ross: 1) Yes — we support an on-prem package where the control plane is customer-managed and Redwood provides the runtime binaries and ops runbooks. 2) For patches we coordinate a maintenance window; we provide signed OS images and you can choose auto-apply or manual approval. Patches are logged and included in the audit bundle.
[08:39] Tom Wu: About signed images — can we verify signatures with our own keyring?
[08:42] Ethan Ross: Yep, images are signed with Redwood's release key by default, but you can add a verification step with your own keyring in the boot process.

[09:00] Maya Patel: I'm going to open the floor for questions. Linda?
[09:03] Linda Park: On SIEM retention — can logs be redacted before leaving the cluster? We need to avoid storing certain PII.
[09:10] Ethan Ross: We support a pre-shipping redaction pipeline that can mask PII fields, or you can opt to send raw logs to your private collector and let your SIEM apply redaction. Redaction at source is preferable for compliance.
[09:22] Linda Park: Who owns redaction rules? We need to ensure change control.
[09:25] Maya Patel: You own rules when configured; we will keep a copy in the audit bundle showing the rule versions.

[09:40] Greg Halvorsen: Any limitations on throughput when encryption is enforced and you use per-tenant clusters?
[09:47] Ethan Ross: There's more overhead per cluster (memory/cold start) but throughput scales almost linearly with dedicated GPUs. We can suggest instance types and batching profiles in Redwood Optimize to keep unit cost predictable.

[10:05] Tom Wu: Practical: what's the minimum lead time to spin up a private cluster in our AWS account with egress proxy, KMS integration, and SIEM shipping?
[10:14] Maya Patel: For a standard private deploy with pre-approved network policies maybe 2–3 weeks. If you need HSM integrations and custom firewall appliances it can push to 4–6 weeks depending on access and approvals.
[10:26] Greg Halvorsen: Ok cool. We need rigid timelines because Q3 audit is scheduled.

[10:35] Ethan Ross: We'll propose a plan: week 1 — design signoff and asset handover; week 2 — infra provisioning and KMS peering; week 3 — pilot with representative traffic and logging; week 4 — review and control mapping.

[10:54] Maya Patel: Now I'll read out a short recap and proposed next steps.
[10:58] Maya Patel: Recap: 1) Airlock pattern with egress proxy and optional fallback to private peering; 2) KMS models (envelope vs HSM API) — you prefer HSM API for strongest control but will evaluate latency; 3) RBAC via SAML group mapping to roles; 4) Audit logs with signed events and WORM storage options; 5) Pilot to validate p95 latency and fallback behavior.
[11:20] Maya Patel: Next steps: we'll send our SOC 2 package, the network diagram, and a proposed pilot plan. Ethan will produce the annotated diagram. We agreed a follow-up control mapping session on 2026-05-28 and a pilot week of 2026-05-31.
[11:34] Linda Park: That works for us. Please include examples of signed audit events and a sample SIEM ingestion config.
[11:40] Ethan Ross: Will do.
[11:42] Greg Halvorsen: We'll share our KMS endpoint and SIEM collector IPs after the meeting.
[11:46] Tom Wu: Also sharing our expected traffic profile so you can size the pilot.
[11:49] Maya Patel: Great, thanks everyone. I'll follow up with notes.
[11:52] Linda Park: Thanks, bye.
[11:54] Greg Halvorsen: Thanks.
[11:56] Ethan Ross: Bye.
